Material Properties
Nitrile
Petroleum oils, fuels, hydraulics. −40 to 120°C. Most common general-purpose seal. Excellent abrasion resistance. Avoid ozone, sunlight, ketones.
Viton
Aggressive chemicals, solvents, fuel additives, high temps to 200°C. Best for harsh environments. More expensive. Poor low-temp flexibility below −20°C.
Silicone
Extreme temps −60 to 230°C. Food/medical-grade available. Excellent UV/ozone resistance. Poor abrasion and tensile strength — static seals only.
EPDM
Water, steam, ozone, UV, brake fluid. −45 to 150°C. Outdoor weathering applications. Not compatible with petroleum oils or fuels — swell severely.
Compression: 20–30% static, 10–25% dynamic. Never exceed 30% — permanent set.
Groove width: 1.5× CS static · 1.4× CS dynamic. Depth = CS × (1 – compression)
Gland surface: Ra <0.8 µm dynamic · Ra <1.6 µm static. Lubricate on install.
Stretch ID over shaft 1–5%. More stretch = lower sealing force. Zero stretch on static face seals.
Never reuse an O-ring removed from service. Cost of a new O-ring is always less than the leak.

Bearing area = π/4 × (OD² − ID²). For plastic substrates, a washer reduces surface stress by 3–10× compared to bare fastener head.
OD should be ≥ 2× bolt diameter for effective load distribution on soft materials.

Split lock washers are not recommended under vibration per NASA/ESA fastener standards — use prevailing torque nuts or Nordlock instead.

External (DIN 471): groove in shaft. Ring snaps in, retains components from sliding off axially.
Internal (DIN 472): groove inside bore. Ring expands into groove, retains components inside bore.
Groove must be machined to spec — rough or undersize groove causes stress concentration and premature failure.
Use correct pliers — external needs tips fitting the lug holes, internal needs expanding tips. Wrong tool = damaged bore.
Never reuse a ring that's been removed — they plastically deform on installation. Keep spares.

GD&T Reference
ASME Y14.5-2018 · Symbols · FCF · Expert rules
The single biggest GD&T win: switch hole locations from ±X/±Y to True Position. A circular tolerance zone has 57% more area than the equivalent square zone — same functional requirement, more parts pass, lower scrap rate. This alone pays for learning GD&T.
★ The Big 5 — Used on 90% of drawings
SymbolNameDatum?What it controlsWhen to use it
⊕True PositionYesLocation of a hole, pin, boss, or slot centerDefault for all hole patterns. Replaces ±X/±Y. Add MMC for clearance holes to get bonus tolerance
⊥PerpendicularityYes90° relationship to datumShafts into bores, pins, press fits. Controls axis squareness on cylinders, face squareness on flat features
⊥⏏FlatnessNoHow flat a surface isSealing faces, mounting surfaces, datums. No datum needed — self-referential
⌓Profile of a SurfaceOpt.3D surface form, orientation, and locationComplex contours, freeform surfaces. Most versatile symbol — can replace many others
↗Circular RunoutYesFIM per cross-section during one revolutionRotating parts: shafts, pulleys, cams. Quick, practical, measurable with a dial indicator
Complete Symbol Reference — ASME Y14.5-2018
SymbolTypeNameDatum?Controls
FORM — no datum required
⏥FormFlatnessNoHow flat a surface is. Inspect with CMM or surface plate. Tighter than size tolerance = impossible to make
⏤FormStraightnessNoStraightness of a line element or axis. Can apply to derived median line (controls bowing of a shaft)
○FormCircularityNoRoundness of each circular cross-section. Does not control axis straightness
⌀FormCylindricityNoRoundness + straightness + taper of a cylinder. Tightest, hardest to inspect form control
PROFILE — datum optional
⌒ProfileOpt.Profile of a LineControls 2D cross-section shape. Use for complex contours, cam profiles, lens edges
⌓ProfileOpt.Profile of a SurfaceControls 3D surface shape. Most versatile — can simultaneously control size, form, orientation, location
ORIENTATION — datum required
∠Orient.YesAngularityControls angle relative to datum. Tolerance zone is two parallel planes. Must have a basic angle dimension
⊥Orient.YesPerpendicularity90° relationship. On shafts controls axis squareness; on surfaces, face squareness
//Orient.YesParallelismParallel surfaces or axes. Used on precision mating faces, rails, ways
LOCATION — datum required
⊕LocationYesTrue PositionMost common. Circular zone = 57% more area than ±. Supports MMC/LMC bonus tolerance. Use for all hole patterns
◎LocationYesConcentricityMedian point alignment. Hard to inspect — use runout or position instead for most applications
⌯LocationYesSymmetryMedian plane alignment. Also difficult to inspect. Removed from ASME 2018 for new designs — use position
RUNOUT — datum required, rotating parts
↗RunoutYesCircular RunoutFIM of each cross-section in one revolution. Quick dial indicator check. Practical for production
⇗RunoutYesTotal RunoutFIM of entire surface in one revolution. Controls both circular and axial variation
Feature Control Frame — How to Read It
⊕ ⌀0.25 Ⓜ A B C
Symbol     Tolerance zone (⌀ = cylindrical)     Modifier     Primary datum     Secondary     Tertiary
  • ⌀ before tolerance means cylindrical zone (use on holes and pins). Without ⌀, zone is two parallel planes (use on tabs, slots, surfaces)
  • Basic dimensions (boxed numbers) locate the true position — they carry no tolerance. The FCF tolerance is the only allowed variation
  • Never mix ± location dimensions with a position FCF on the same feature — they create conflicting instructions that confuse inspectors
  • Title block must specify the standard — write "ASME Y14.5-2018" or "ISO 1101-2017". Interpretation rules differ between standards
Modifier Guide — MMC / LMC / RFS
SymbolNameBonus tolerance?Use when...Don't use when...
ⓂMMCYes — as hole grows bigger than MMCClearance holes in bolt patterns. Assembly is only concernPress fits, interference fits, rotating features
ⓁLMCYes — as hole gets smaller than LMCMinimum wall thickness control, thin bossesMost common applications — rarely needed
ⓈRFSNo — tolerance is fixedDefault (no symbol needed). Rotating parts, press fits, any case where bonus tolerance is unacceptableN/A — this is the safe default
PProjectedDepends on baseLong studs, pins — extend zone above the mating surface where the mating part sees the errorShort fasteners, standard through-holes
True Position Deep Dive — The Most Important Symbol
  • 57% more area than ±X/±Y — a ±0.1mm square zone and a ø0.283mm circular zone accept exactly the same parts at the corners, but the circular zone accepts 57% more valid parts between the corners. Same function, more yield
  • Floating fastener formula: tolerance = hole clearance — T = H − F (hole MMC diameter minus fastener max diameter). Start here for every bolt pattern
  • Fixed fastener formula: T = (H − F) / 2 when both parts have threaded holes (no floating). Each part gets half the clearance
  • MMC bonus on clearance holes: if hole MMC is ø4.0mm and actual is ø4.1mm, you get 0.1mm bonus position tolerance. This is free tolerance — use it
  • Functional gages vs CMM: at >50 parts, a go/no-go functional gage is 5–10× faster than CMM inspection per part. Design the gage at the same time as the drawing
  • Scrap reduction: switching a 4-hole pattern from ±X/±Y to true position at MMC typically reduces scrap rate by 3–8% on CNC aluminum parts
Datum Reference Frame — 3-2-1 Rule
  • Primary datum (A) — largest flat surface, constrains 3 DOF (3-point contact). Always choose the most important functional surface
  • Secondary datum (B) — long edge or bore, constrains 2 DOF (2-point contact). The part's longest stable edge
  • Tertiary datum (C) — short edge or single point, constrains 1 DOF. Stops rotation about the B axis
  • Simulate assembly fixtures — your datum scheme should mirror how the part is fixtured in manufacturing and held during use
  • Qualify your datums — add flatness to primary datum A, straightness or cylindricity to datum bores. An unqualified datum propagates form error into every downstream tolerance
  • Curved surfaces as datums — use only with a clear functional reason. Curved surface datums require specialized fixturing and are hard to inspect consistently
⚠ The 10 Most Expensive GD&T Mistakes
  • Using ±X/±Y for hole locations — creates square zones, wastes 57% of your tolerance, causes false rejects. Switch to true position with basic dimensions
  • Flatness tighter than size tolerance — if a face has a ±0.05mm size tolerance, flatness <0.1mm is geometrically impossible. The size tolerance already contains the form
  • No datum on orientation callouts — angularity or perpendicularity without a datum reference is not a valid callout per ASME Y14.5. The FCF has no meaning without knowing what it's perpendicular to
  • Using concentricity or symmetry when runout/position works — these require finding the derived median line or median plane. A CMM programmer nightmare. Use circular runout or true position instead — same functional result, 5× easier to inspect
  • MMC on press-fit holes — bonus tolerance is wrong here. The size dimension already controls interference. Adding MMC gives position error as the hole gets bigger, which you don't want in a press fit
  • Over-tolerancing non-functional features — applying ±0.025mm to a cosmetic face costs 3–5× more in machining with zero functional benefit. Only tighten where it matters for fit, function, or assembly
  • Redundant controls — calling out both flatness and parallelism to the same surface with the same tolerance value adds no information and confuses inspectors
  • No GD&T standard called out in title block — ASME Y14.5 and ISO 1101 interpret some callouts differently. Without specifying, suppliers and inspectors guess
  • Missing or ambiguous datum references — "A" on the drawing must be clearly identified with a datum triangle. Vague datum placement is the single most common source of CMM setup disputes
  • Process-specific tolerance mismatch — applying CNC tolerances (±0.025mm) to injection-molded or sheet metal features. Know your process capability: IM = ±0.1–0.3mm, sheet metal = ±0.3–0.5mm, CNC = ±0.013–0.1mm

FAQ — Most Asked Questions
  • Q: When should I use GD&T instead of ± tolerances? Always for hole patterns (use position), always for rotating parts (use runout), always for mating surfaces (use flatness/perpendicularity). Use ± only for overall envelope dimensions where there's no geometric relationship to control
  • Q: How do I pick a position tolerance value? Use the floating fastener formula: T = hole diameter − fastener diameter. Never guess. A 4mm bolt in a 4.3mm hole gives position tolerance of ø0.3mm total, split equally between both mating parts
  • Q: What is a basic dimension? A boxed number on a drawing that locates or orients a GD&T tolerance zone. It has no tolerance of its own — all variation is specified in the FCF. Do not add ± to a basic dimension
  • Q: Can I use runout instead of concentricity? Yes, for almost all applications. Runout is easier to measure (dial indicator), and total runout controls coaxiality just as well. Concentricity requires finding the median axis — a much harder inspection operation
  • Q: What's the difference between circularity and cylindricity? Circularity controls each cross-section independently (roundness of a slice). Cylindricity controls the whole cylinder — roundness + straightness + taper simultaneously. Cylindricity is harder to inspect and rarely needed unless the whole surface is a precision bearing surface
  • Q: When does profile replace all other callouts? Profile of a Surface is the Swiss Army knife of GD&T — it can control size, form, orientation, and location in one callout. Best for freeform surfaces, complex contours, and any surface where a single unified tolerance makes more sense than multiple individual controls

ISO Fits & Tolerances
ISO 286 · Common shaft/hole fits
H7/g6 is the go-to clearance fit for precision shafts. H7/p6 gives reliable press fit with steel; use H7/u6 for aluminium hubs (higher interference needed). Always verify interference with a press-fit calc — thin-walled hubs can split. K/k transitions are good for parts needing easy removal but no slop.

Key Rules
  1. Hole-basis (H) is preferred — bores are harder to hold than shafts.
  2. For aluminium hubs with steel shafts, increase interference 30–50% (Al expands more).
  3. Verify with press-fit calc — thin hubs can split at H7/p6.
  4. Interference for grey cast iron — use 30% of steel values.
  5. For plastic-to-metal press fits, use H7/r6 max and check creep relaxation.

FAQ
  • Q: Which fit should I use for a locating dowel pin? H7/h6 for hand-press fit (zero to slight clearance), H7/k6 if you need a light mallet, H7/p6 for a permanent press. Default locating: H7/h6.
  • Q: Why is the hole-basis system preferred? Bores are harder to hit precisely than shafts. In hole-basis (H), the hole is fixed and the shaft is adjusted — you only need standard reamers and boring bars for the hole side.
  • Q: What fit for a bearing in a housing? Tight transition to light press: H7/k6 or H7/m6 for bearing outer race in aluminum. Steel housings can go H7/p6. Never a clearance fit for a rotating bearing outer race.
  • Q: What's the difference between IT6 and IT7? About 1.6× more tolerance in IT7. IT7 is achievable with standard CNC. IT6 requires precision grinding or honing. For most assemblies, IT7 is the right call — tighter costs more with marginal benefit.
  • Q: How do I calculate the actual clearance for H7/g6 at 25mm? H7 hole: +0 to +0.021mm. g6 shaft: −0.007 to −0.020mm. Min clearance = 0.007mm, max clearance = 0.041mm. Use the ISO fit calculator in the Calcs tab to verify.
  • Q: Do fits apply to plastic parts? ISO 286 is defined for metal. For plastic-to-metal or plastic-to-plastic, add 0.1–0.3mm to the clearance to account for moisture absorption (Nylon) and thermal expansion differences. Never assume plastic holds IT7 tolerance without testing.

Critical Rules for Metal Design
  • Always specify alloy + temper — 6061-T6 vs 6061-O have yield strengths of 276MPa vs 55MPa. Temper is not optional information
  • Galvanic coupling — Al + SS fasteners in any wet environment = guaranteed corrosion. Voltage difference >0.5V in electrolyte = use nylon isolators or anodize the Al boss
  • Machinability cost scaling — 303 SS costs 2.5x more to machine than 6061-T6. Ti costs 5-8x more. 316L is "gummy" and work-hardens — budget separately
  • Weldability restrictions — 303, 2024, and 7075 are not weldable. 6061 welds fine but loses temper in the HAZ — re-heat-treat or redesign if strength is critical there
  • Passivate machined stainless — machining contaminates the surface with iron particles that rust. ASTM A967 passivation restores the protective oxide layer. Specify it on every SS drawing
  • Hot-rolled vs cold-rolled steel — HR has scale and looser tolerances. CR has better surface, tighter tolerance, slight work-hardening. Specify CRS for machined parts, HRS for welded structures

Critical Rules for Plastic Design
  • Nylon absorbs moisture — PA6 absorbs 2-9% water by weight. Properties are measured dry. Real service properties are 20-40% lower. Design with wet dimensions. Condition parts before final assembly inspection
  • HDT is not service temperature — Heat Deflection Temperature is measured under 1.82MPa load. Real service temperature for structural parts is 20-30C below HDT
  • Shrinkage drives tolerances — Semicrystalline (PP, Nylon, POM) shrinks 1.5-3%. Amorphous (ABS, PC) shrinks 0.4-0.7%. Glass fill reduces shrink but makes it directional along flow
  • Glass fill kills ductility — 30% GF raises stiffness 2-3x but makes material brittle. Never use GF in snap fits, living hinges, or impact zones. Use unfilled or rubber-toughened grades instead
  • UL94 must be specified explicitly — Standard ABS is UL94 HB (horizontal burn). Electronics enclosures require V-0 or V-1. Specify the UL94 rating in the material call-out, not just the base resin name
  • Uniform wall thickness is the #1 DFM rule — Vary wall by no more than 25% of nominal. Thick sections sink, warp, extend cycle time, and increase part cost. Core out anything over 5mm nominal
  • Color specification prevents supplier chaos — "Matte black" from 5 suppliers = 5 different colors. Specify Pantone + RAL + L*a*b* values with D65 illuminant and 10 degree observer
Plastic vs Metal Decision Guide
  • Choose plastic when: complex geometry, volume >500 units, non-structural, electrical insulation needed, weight is critical, or per-unit cost drives the decision
  • Choose machined metal when: high mechanical load, temp >150C continuous, tight tolerances (<0.05mm), EMI shielding required, or low volume (<200 units)
  • Choose die cast Al when: metal enclosure with complex geometry at volume (>5k units). Better dimensional control than sheet metal, better cosmetics than cast iron, cheaper per-part than machined
  • Never substitute industrial for medical-grade plastic: same base polymer in different grades may have completely different additive packages, colorants, and processing aids — all of which affect biocompatibility

Material Properties
Nitrile
Petroleum oils, fuels, hydraulics. −40 to 120°C. Most common general-purpose seal. Excellent abrasion resistance. Avoid ozone, sunlight, ketones.
Viton
Aggressive chemicals, solvents, fuel additives, high temps to 200°C. Best for harsh environments. More expensive. Poor low-temp flexibility below −20°C.
Silicone
Extreme temps −60 to 230°C. Food/medical-grade available. Excellent UV/ozone resistance. Poor abrasion and tensile strength — static seals only.
EPDM
Water, steam, ozone, UV, brake fluid. −45 to 150°C. Outdoor weathering applications. Not compatible with petroleum oils or fuels — swell severely.
Compression: 20–30% static, 10–25% dynamic. Never exceed 30% — permanent set.
Groove width: 1.5× CS static · 1.4× CS dynamic. Depth = CS × (1 – compression)
Gland surface: Ra <0.8 µm dynamic · Ra <1.6 µm static. Lubricate on install.
Stretch ID over shaft 1–5%. More stretch = lower sealing force. Zero stretch on static face seals.
Never reuse an O-ring removed from service. Cost of a new O-ring is always less than the leak.

GD&T Symbols
ASME Y14.5 · ISO 1101
GD&T controls geometry independently from size tolerances. Use form controls (flatness, circularity) without datums; orientation and location need at least one. Tip: for consumer products, true position on a pattern is almost always better than ±X/±Y — it gives 57% more tolerance zone area.
Symbol Reference · ASME Y14.5-2018
SymbolCharTypeDatum?Controls
Flatness⏥FormNoHow flat a surface is. Inspect with a CMM or surface plate.
Straightness⏤FormNoStraightness of a line element or axis. Can be applied to a derived median line.
Circularity○FormNoRoundness of each circular cross-section. Does not control axis.
Cylindricity⌀FormNoCombines roundness + straightness + taper. Tightest form control.
Profile of a Line⌒ProfileOpt.Controls 2D cross-section shape. Used for complex contours.
Profile of a Surface⌓ProfileOpt.Controls 3D surface shape. Most versatile control — can replace many others.
Angularity∠Orient.YesControls angle relative to datum. Tolerance zone is two parallel planes.
Perpendicularity⊥Orient.Yes90° relationship. On shafts controls axis squareness; on surfaces, face squareness.
Parallelism//Orient.YesParallel surfaces or axes. Often used on precision mating faces.
True Position⊕LocationYesMost common callout. Circular tolerance zone — 57% more area than ±X/±Y. Supports MMC/LMC.
Concentricity◎LocationYesMedian point alignment. Very hard to inspect — use runout instead for most applications.
Symmetry⌯LocationYesControls median plane alignment. Also difficult to inspect. Often replaced by profile.
Circular Runout↗RunoutYesFIM of each cross-section in one revolution. Quick, practical check for rotating parts.
Total Runout⇗RunoutYesFIM of entire surface in one revolution. Controls both circular and axial variation.
Feature Control Frame Anatomy
  • A FCF reads left-to-right: [Symbol] | [Tolerance value] | [Modifier] | [Datum A] | [Datum B] | [Datum C].
  • The ⌀ before a tolerance means the zone is cylindrical (used with position on a hole).
  • MMC modifier (Ⓜ) adds bonus tolerance — if a hole is 0.1mm bigger than MMC, you get 0.1mm of extra position tolerance.
Modifier Quick Guide
SymbolNameWhen to Use
ⓂMMCClearance holes in assemblies — gives extra tolerance at largest shaft / smallest hole
ⓁLMCMin wall thickness, press fits — tightens as feature gets smaller
ⓈRFSDefault (no symbol). Applies regardless of actual size. Required for rotating parts.
⊕ProjectedLong studs/pins — extends tolerance zone above the mating surface
Datum Reference Frame Rules
  • Primary datum constrains the most DOF (usually a flat face — 3 points).
  • Secondary constrains 2 DOF (long edge — 2 points).
  • Tertiary constrains 1 DOF (short edge — 1 point).
  • The 3-2-1 rule.
  • Always simulate how the part physically sits in its fixture — that's your datum scheme.
  • Avoid using curved surfaces as primary datums unless you have a specific reason.
Common GD&T Mistakes
  1. Using ±X/±Y tolerances on hole patterns — switches to true position to get the circular zone.
  2. Adding flatness tighter than the size tolerance — impossible to make.
  3. Over-constraining with too many datums — 3 datums define a complete coordinate system; more is redundant.
  4. Specifying concentricity/symmetry when runout/position would work — makes inspection 10× harder.
  5. No datum on orientation callouts — angularity without a datum is not a valid callout.
Further Reading
GD&T Basics — Symbol Guide ↗ InspectionXpert — GD&T Reference ↗ ASME Y14.5-2018 Standard ↗
ISO Fits & Tolerances
ISO 286 · Common shaft/hole fits
H7/g6 is the go-to clearance fit for precision shafts. H7/p6 gives reliable press fit with steel; use H7/u6 for aluminium hubs (higher interference needed). Always verify interference with a press-fit calc — thin-walled hubs can split. K/k transitions are good for parts needing easy removal but no slop.
ISO 286 Fit Classes (∅10–50mm typical)
ClassDesignationClearance mmUse Case
Loose runningH11/c11+0.06 to +0.33Wide clearance — dirty environments, linkages, agricultural
Free runningH9/d9+0.02 to +0.10Lubricated journals, general rotating fits
Close runningH8/f7+0.01 to +0.05Precision journals, spindles with light lubrication
Sliding ★H7/g6+0.002 to +0.025Slide without perceptible play. Most common precision fit.
Locating (clearance)H7/h60 to +0.021Accurate location, hand-assembly. Good for dowel pins.
Locating (transition)H7/k6−0.006 to +0.015Accurate location, may need mallet. Bushings, hubs.
Transition (tight)H7/n6−0.012 to +0.009Tight transition. Keyed hubs, requires press or heating.
Press (light)H7/p6−0.006 to −0.029Light interference — permanent for steel. Good starting point.
Press (medium)H7/s6−0.017 to −0.048Standard press for gears, pulleys, sleeves on steel shafts.
Force / shrinkH7/u6−0.031 to −0.072Heavy interference — requires heating hub or chilling shaft.
Tolerance Grade Comparison (IT grades)
IT GradeTolerance ∅25mmTypical Process
IT50.009mmFine grinding, honing
IT60.013mmPrecision CNC turning/milling
IT70.021mmStandard CNC machining ← most common
IT80.033mmStandard turning, reaming
IT90.052mmRough turning, boring
IT110.130mmStamping, die casting
Key Rules
  1. Hole-basis (H) is preferred — bores are harder to hold than shafts.
  2. For aluminium hubs with steel shafts, increase interference 30–50% (Al expands more).
  3. Verify with press-fit calc — thin hubs can split at H7/p6.
  4. Interference for grey cast iron — use 30% of steel values.
  5. For plastic-to-metal press fits, use H7/r6 max and check creep relaxation.

DFM Rules
Injection · CNC · Sheet Metal
The single biggest DFM cost saver: eliminate undercuts. Each undercut typically adds $3–15k in tooling (side actions or lifters). Wall thickness uniformity prevents sink and warp — keep within 25% of nominal. Boss diameter should be 2× screw OD; rib thickness 60% of wall.

Surface Finish Ra
ISO 1302 · µm & µin · N grades
Ra 1.6µm (N7) is "machined" — the default for most functional surfaces. Ra 0.8µm (N6) for bearing seats and sealing faces. Ra 3.2µm (N8) for non-functional machined faces. For injection moulding, SPI-A2 (Ra ~0.05µm) is high gloss; SPI-B1 (Ra ~0.4µm) is semi-gloss for most consumer housings.
Ra / N Grade Reference
Ra µmN GradeRa µinProcessKey Uses
0.025N11Superfinish / lappingGauge surfaces, optical
0.05N22Cylindrical grindPrecision bearing seats
0.1N34Fine grind / honeHydraulic cylinder bores
0.4N516Fine turnO-ring grooves ← sealing minimum
0.8N632Finish turn / millBearing seats, sealing faces
1.6 ★N763CNC turn / millStandard machined — most common default
3.2N8125Rough turnNon-functional machined faces
6.3N9250Rough mill / sawClearance surfaces, unmachined flash
12.5N10500Casting / forgingSand casting, rough weld
SPI Injection Mould Grades
SPIRa approxMethodLook
A-10.012 µmDiamond buff #3Mirror — lens quality
A-20.025 µmDiamond buff #6High gloss consumer electronics
A-30.05 µmDiamond buff #15General high gloss
B-1~0.1 µm600 grit paperSemi-gloss — most housings
B-2~0.2 µm400 grit paperLow gloss
C-1~0.4 µm600 grit stoneSatin / industrial
D-1~0.8 µmDry blast glass beadMatt textured
D-3~3.2 µmDry blast Al oxideRough — hides sink marks
Sealing Surface Rules
  • O-ring bore: 0.4–0.8 µm Ra (N5–N6).
  • Too smooth (< 0.2 µm) traps a hydraulic film and prevents proper sealing — the o-ring won't conform.
  • Too rough (> 1.6 µm) damages the elastomer on assembly and during cycling.
  • Flat-face gasket seating: 0.8–1.6 µm Ra.
  • Dynamic rod seals: 0.1–0.4 µm Ra with lay perpendicular to motion.
  • Avoid circumferential lay marks on seal bores — they create leak paths.
Drawing Callouts
  • Use the ISO 1302 triangle symbol. "All over" (AO) default can be set in the title block — anything tighter gets an individual callout.
  • Always specify Ra (arithmetic mean) not Rz (peak-to-valley) for machined parts unless you specifically need to control peak heights.
  • Rz ≈ 4–7× Ra for most machined surfaces.
FAQ
  • Q: What surface finish should I spec as a default on machined parts? Ra 1.6 µm (N7, 63 µin) for general machined surfaces. Specify tighter only where there's a functional reason: sealing, bearing seats, or sliding fits.
  • Q: What Ra do I need for an o-ring bore? 0.4–0.8 µm Ra (N5–N6). Below 0.2 µm is too smooth — the o-ring won't compress. Above 1.6 µm damages the elastomer. This is the most common sealing surface mistake.
  • Q: What's the difference between Ra and Rz? Ra is arithmetic mean roughness (average). Rz is mean peak-to-valley height. Rz is 4–7× Ra for typical machined surfaces. Specify Ra for most applications. Use Rz when you specifically care about peak heights (e.g., sealing or tribology).
  • Q: Do I need to specify surface finish on every surface? No. Set a "general" default in the title block (typically Ra 3.2 or 1.6 µm), then callout individual surfaces that are tighter. Only call out what matters functionally.
  • Q: What SPI grade for a consumer electronics housing? B-1 (600 grit paper) for semi-gloss. A-2 or A-3 for high-gloss. D-1 for matte/satin. A-1 only for optical components — it adds significant tooling cost.
  • Q: Can surface finish be improved after machining? Yes. Vibratory deburring, bead blasting, hand polishing, or superfinishing can improve Ra significantly. Factor post-processing into lead time and cost. Anodize does not improve surface finish — it follows the substrate exactly.

Hardness Conversion
HRC · HV · HB · UTS
Quick rule: UTS (MPa) ≈ HB × 3.5 for steel. HRC 58–62 is typical for cutting tools; HRC 40–50 for general tooling; HRC 20–30 for structural parts. Above HRC 40, machinability drops sharply — specify hardness after machining unless geometry requires pre-hardened stock.
Hardness Conversion Table (steel)
HRCHVHBUTS MPaReal-World Example
65+832+——HSS/carbide cutting tools
62746——File, Grade 12.9 bolt core
58655—~2200Case-hardened gear tooth
50513—~1800Spring steel, die faces
45446425~1550Set screws, hardened shafts
40392371~1350Grade 10.9 bolt, tooling steel
35345327~1150Grade 8.8 bolt
30302286~1000Stainless A4-80 fasteners
20226213~740Structural mild steel, 1020
—120114~4006061-T6 aluminium
—8076~280Free-machining brass
Scale Applicability
ScaleIndenterLoadBest For
HRCDiamond cone150 kgfHard steels (>HRC 20)
HRB1/16" ball100 kgfSoft materials, Al, brass (up to HRB 100)
HV (Vickers)Diamond pyramid1–100 kgfUniversal, thin sections, case depth
HB (Brinell)10mm ball3000 kgfLarge castings, forgings — not hard steel
Shore ABlunt cone—Elastomers, soft plastics (0–100A)
Shore DSharp cone—Hard plastics, rubbers (>Shore A 90)
Practical Rules
  1. UTS (MPa) ≈ HB × 3.45 for steel (±10%).
  2. Above HRC 40, conventional machining becomes expensive — EDM or grind after hardening.
  3. Case hardening (carburizing, nitriding) gives a hard surface over a tough core — ideal for gears and shafts. Specify case depth (typically 0.5–2mm) and core hardness separately.
  4. Measuring HRC on thin stock or thin case gives false-low readings — use HV with low load (HV 0.3 or HV 1) for thin sections.
  5. Never weld HRC 40+ without pre/post heat treatment.

FAQ
  • Q: When should I specify HRC vs HV vs HB? HRC for hard steels (>HRC 20). HB for large castings and forgings. HV when you need universal comparison, thin sections, or case depth measurement. Never use HRC on thin stock or plating — you'll get a false-low reading.
  • Q: How hard can I machine steel? Up to ~HRC 40 with carbide tooling and the right feeds/speeds. Above HRC 45, machining becomes very expensive. Above HRC 55, typically grind or EDM only. Design: machine soft, then heat treat, then grind critical features.
  • Q: What's the correct sequence for hardened parts? Machine soft (annealed) → heat treat to spec → grind/finish critical bores and faces. Never cut threads after hardening — roll them before, or cut them before and mask them during heat treat.
  • Q: What hardness for a gear? Case-hardened tooth face: HRC 58–62 with tough core HRC 28–35. Specify both: "Case harden to HRC 58–62 min 0.8mm depth, core HRC 30–38." Tooth surface must be hard; root must be tough to resist bending fatigue.
  • Q: How do I convert between scales? Use ASTM E140 conversion tables. The calc in this app converts between HRC, HV, HB, and UTS. Note: conversions are approximate (±5%) and only valid within the scale's recommended range.
Thermal Management
Heatsink · TIM · Derating
Thermal resistance is additive like electrical resistance. A 1°C/W heatsink with 0.5°C/W TIM and 5°C/W junction-to-case gives 6.5°C/W total. At 5W that's a 32.5°C rise. TIM matters: bare metal contact is ~5°C/W; quality thermal paste is 0.3–0.8°C/W; phase-change pads are a middle ground.
ConceptFormula / RuleTypical
Thermal resistanceRθ = ΔT / P (°C/W)Lower = better
Junction tempTj = Ta + P × RθjaTj < Tjmax − 15°C
Heatsink sizingRθsa = (Tjmax−Ta)/P − Rθjc − RθcsBudget 10°C spreading
Natural convection~10–25W at Rθ 2–5°C/WFin area ≥50 cm²/W
Forced air~1–3°C/W at 1–3 m/sFan CFM = 2× free-air
TIMk W/m·KBondline µmBest For
Thermal paste8.550–100CPU/heatsink
Phase-change pad3–650–150Production
Thermal pad3.0500–2000PCB-to-chassis
Indium foil82100–250Ultra-high-power
Heatsink Design Rules
  • Natural convection: fin spacing ≥ 6mm, fin height ≤ 50mm, vertical orientation preferred.
  • Forced air: fin spacing 2–4mm.
  • Black anodize adds 5–10% radiation benefit above 60°C delta-T.
  • Thermal vias through PCB: min 0.3mm dia, 1mm pitch, copper-filled — reduce board thermal resistance by 30–60%.
  • Always place thermal vias directly under high-power IC pads, not beside them.
Derating Rules
  • Design for Tj ≤ Tjmax − 15°C at max ambient.
  • Never run components at 100% rated temp in a production product — thermal resistance increases with age.
  • Capacitors: derate voltage by 50% and temperature by 20°C for life.
  • MOSFETs: Rds(on) increases ~2× from 25°C to 100°C — size for hot, not cold.
  • Batteries: capacity drops ~20% at 0°C; charge only above 0°C for Li-ion.

FAQ
  • Q: How do I size a heatsink? Rθsa = (Tjmax − Tambient) / P − Rθjc − Rθcs. Calculate total thermal budget, subtract junction-to-case and TIM resistances, what's left is the heatsink spec. Use this as a target for your heatsink selection or design.
  • Q: What's the best TIM for production? Phase-change pad (3–6 W/m·K) for most production — repeatable, no pump-out, no mess. Thermal grease has the lowest resistance but pumps out over thermal cycles. Indium foil for extreme power density where cost isn't a concern.
  • Q: Do I need thermal simulation? Yes for any product with components running >60°C delta-T or in a sealed enclosure. Simulation (Ansys Icepak, COMSOL, or even free FloTHERM XT lite) catches heatsink inadequacy and hotspot locations before proto. Changes after EVT are expensive.
  • Q: How does altitude affect cooling? Air density drops at altitude — natural convection is 15–30% less effective at 3,000m. If your product operates at altitude, derate natural convection accordingly or shift to conduction cooling. Forced air is less affected but fan performance also drops.
  • Q: Why do my components fail early even though they're within rated temp? Thermal resistance increases with age (TIM dry-out, oxidation). Always design with 15°C margin below Tjmax. Also check: are you measuring case temp or junction temp? Case temp can be 15–30°C below junction at high power.
Galvanic & Finishing
Corrosion series · Surface treatments
The galvanic series in seawater: gold → platinum → titanium → stainless 316 → copper → brass → bronze → tin → lead → steel → aluminum → zinc → magnesium. Farther apart = more aggressive galvanic attack on the anodic (less noble) metal. Isolate dissimilar metals with nylon washers or coatings. Anodize aluminum before mating with steel fasteners.
MetalPotential VNotes
Gold / Platinum+1.2 to +1.5Most noble — cathode
316 SS (passive)+0.0 to +0.2Passive film critical
Copper / Brass−0.2 to −0.4OK vs steel; not vs Al (wet)
Steel (carbon)−0.5 to −0.7Use anti-seize vs Al
6061 Aluminium−0.7 to −0.8Anodize for protection
Zinc / Galv. steel−0.9 to −1.1Sacrificial anode
TreatmentMaterialµmSalt spray hrs
Type II AnodizeAl5–25336–500
Type III Hard AnodizeAl25–751000+
Zinc plateSteel8–12200–500
Electroless NiSteel/Al5–25500–1000
Powder coatSteel/Al50–100500–2000
Isolation Methods
MethodBest ForNotes
Nylon washer + sleeveBolt isolationMust isolate shank too — washer alone not enough
Alodine / AloditeAl structural jointsConductive, paintable, cheap — not a substitute for anodize
Type II anodizeAl-to-steel jointsInsulating — breaks galvanic path at fastener holes
Anti-seize compoundStainless-to-Al threadsPrevents galling + slows galvanic attack
Sealant at jointOutdoor assembliesEliminates electrolyte bridge — most effective method
Material Selection for Corrosion Environments
  • Marine/coastal: 316 SS (not 304 — Cl⁻ pits 304 rapidly), 6061 with Type III hard anodize, HDPE hardware.
  • Consumer outdoor: every M4 stainless into bare 6061 is a corrosion clock — anodize or isolate.
  • Medical devices: passivated 316L or Ti Grade 5 for implant-adjacent parts.
  • High temp (>150°C): Inconel, Ti, or ceramic coatings — most electroplating fails above 200°C.
  • Carbon fiber composites: always electrically isolate from metal — CF is cathodic and aggressive.
FAQ
  • Q: Can I use stainless steel fasteners in an aluminum housing? Yes, but isolate them. M4 SS fastener into bare 6061 in an outdoor/coastal product = galvanic corrosion within months. Add a nylon washer + nylon sleeve on the shank, and apply anti-corrosion compound to the thread.
  • Q: Is 304 or 316 stainless better for outdoor products? 316L. The molybdenum addition in 316L resists chloride pitting that 304 is susceptible to in coastal or humid environments. If the product ever sees salt air, 316L is mandatory. 303 is not suitable for outdoor exposure at all.
  • Q: What's the best coating to prevent galvanic corrosion on aluminum? Type III hard anodize (25–75µm) for the highest protection. Type II for general use. Alodine (Alodite, chromate conversion) for conductive joints where you need electrical contact. For marine: Type III + sealant.
  • Q: Does carbon fiber cause galvanic corrosion? Yes — aggressively. CF is cathodic and highly conductive. Always electrically isolate CFRP from metal with fiberglass fabric, PTFE film, or non-conductive adhesive. This is a common failure mode in lightweight structural assemblies.
  • Q: How long does zinc plating last outdoors? 8–12µm trivalent zinc plate: 200–500 hours salt spray per ASTM B117. Real-world: 1–3 years in mild environments, months in coastal. For longer life: zinc-nickel plate (1,000+ hours), or powder coat over zinc.

Manufacturing Methods
Process · Volume · Tolerance
Choose process by volume: FDM/SLA for 1–20 parts; urethane casting for 20–200; injection mould at 500+. CNC tolerances: ±0.05mm is standard, ±0.01mm is precision and costs 3–5×. Sheet metal: laser cut to ±0.1mm, bent to ±0.5°. Die casting tolerances are tighter than injection moulding but limited to non-ferrous metals.

Sheet Metal1–100k±0.1–0.3mm3–7 days
Inj. Molding1k–1M+±0.05–0.1mm4–12 wks

Process Selection Guide
  1. Use FDM/SLA for fit-check and concept validation — never quote tolerances off a print for final design.
  2. MJF/SLS gives isotropic properties unlike FDM; good for functional prototypes.
  3. Urethane casting (RTV tooling) for 20–200 production-like parts in 2–3 weeks — excellent bridge before injection moulding.
  4. 3-axis CNC is 3–5× cheaper than 5-axis — design parts that can be fixtured simply.
  5. Die casting requires 1–3° draft, 2–4mm wall minimum, and accepts embedded inserts. Much tighter dimensional control than injection moulding for metal parts.
  6. Sheet metal — K-factor 0.41 for Al, 0.44 for steel. Minimum bend radius = 1× material thickness for Al, 0.5× for steel.

Die casting$20–150k$2–15$0.50–5

DFM Checklist — Before Tool Release
  • Draft angles: 1° min on untextured, 3° min on textured surfaces.
  • Wall thickness: ±25% of nominal max — thick-to-thin transitions cause sink.
  • Undercuts: eliminate or design in side actions before quoting.
  • Gate location: place in thick section, away from cosmetic faces and structural features.
  • Ribs: height ≤ 3× nominal wall, thickness 50–60% of nominal wall.
  • Bosses: wall 60% of nominal, gussets to base.
  • Parting line: define explicitly on drawing — toolmaker will choose worst location if not specified.
Common DFM Mistakes by Process
ProcessMost Common MistakeFix
Injection moldVariable wall thicknessCore out thick sections; keep ±25% of nominal
Injection moldNo draft on textureAdd 3–5° per 0.025mm texture depth
CNCDeep narrow slotsWidth ≥ 1.5× depth; specify end mill dia on drawing
CNCTight tolerance on wrong featureOnly tolerance what matters — tight tols on non-functional features cost money
Sheet metalBend radius too tightMin radius = 1× material thickness for steel, 1.5× for Al
Sheet metalHoles too close to bendMin distance = 2× material thickness + bend radius
Die castingWall too thin at junctionMin 2mm Al, uniform at junction — porosity forms at transitions
Urethane castOver-tolerancingUrethane is ±0.5mm typical — don't spec ±0.1mm

FAQ
  • Q: How do I pick between processes at low volume? 1–10 units: CNC or 3D print. 10–200: CNC or urethane cast. 200–1,000: urethane cast or soft (Al) injection mold tool. 1,000+: production injection mold. Volume is the primary driver; geometry complexity is secondary.
  • Q: How much does a DFM review cost? Most CMs offer free DFM review with an RFQ — take advantage of this every time. A DFM issue caught at RFQ costs zero. The same issue found at T1 costs $2,000–20,000 and 2–8 weeks.
  • Q: When does a 5-axis CNC justify itself? When part geometry requires undercuts, compound angles, or multi-face machining that would require 4+ setups on 3-axis. Not for cosmetic reasons. 3-axis is 3–5× cheaper — only go 5-axis when the geometry demands it.
  • Q: What's the actual cost breakdown for injection molding? Tooling: $8–100k (one-time). Resin: $1–15/kg. Cycle time: 15–60 seconds depending on part. Per-unit cost at 10k: $0.50–$10. Break-even vs CNC: typically 300–1,000 units depending on part size and complexity.
  • Q: What file format should I send to a manufacturer? STEP (.stp) is the universal standard for 3D geometry. IGES as backup. PDF drawing for tolerances, notes, and surface finishes. Never send STL for machined parts — it loses geometric precision. Always send a drawing with the STEP.

Product Certifications
CE · FCC · UL · FDA · RoHS
CE marking is self-declaration in the EU — you write a Declaration of Conformity. FCC is also self-declaration for Part 15 devices. UL certification requires lab testing and ongoing factory audits. Budget 3–6 months and $15–80k for CE+FCC on a typical IoT product. Get compliance into your design before EVT — retroactive fixes are expensive.

Pre-Compliance Strategy
  1. Use a pre-certified radio module (ESP32, nRF52840, Murata, u-blox) — you inherit the FCC/IC grant for the radio, only need to test conducted and radiated for the system. Saves $10–20k and 6–8 weeks.
  2. Run an EMC pre-scan at EVT — most major CM cities have labs. Budget $2–5k.
  3. Ferrites, ground planes, and PCB stackup changes are cheap before tooling sign-off, expensive after.
  4. CE — use harmonised standards (RED Directive for wireless: EN 300 328, EN 301 489; LVD: EN 62368-1).
  5. Safety certification (UL, TUV) applies to power-connected products — battery-only devices have lower bar.

FAQ
  • Q: Do I need FCC certification to sell a product in the US? Yes, if your product has any intentional or unintentional radio frequency emitter. This includes Bluetooth, WiFi, cellular, and any digital clock above 9kHz that could radiate. Purely passive products (no electronics) are exempt.
  • Q: What's the cheapest path to CE marking for a wireless product? Use a pre-certified module (ESP32, Nordic nRF52, Murata, u-blox). You inherit the radio certification. You still need to test your complete system for conducted/radiated emissions per EN 300 328 and EN 301 489. Total cost: $5–15k vs $25–50k for a custom radio design.
  • Q: How long does FCC certification take? TCB (Telecommunication Certification Body) route: 2–6 weeks with a pre-certified module, 8–16 weeks for a custom radio design. Budget for one re-test cycle. Start certification 3 months before your target launch date minimum.
  • Q: Do I need UL certification? UL certification is voluntary but practically required for retail (Best Buy, Amazon, major retailers require it). Battery-powered products need IEC 62133. Mains-powered products need UL 62368-1 (audio/video/IT) or UL 60950. Medical products have specific UL standards.
  • Q: What is an NDA (Notice of Apparent Liability)? An FCC enforcement action. Selling an uncertified radio product in the US can result in $10,000–100,000+ per violation fines. Don't ship without certification. Amazon will delist uncertified products and increasingly requires proof of certification at listing.

IP Ratings
IEC 60529 · Ingress protection decoder
IP67 = dust-tight + 1m submersion for 30 min. IP68 = dust-tight + deeper/longer submersion (manufacturer-specified). Gasket compression is critical: o-ring groove depth should give 15–25% compression. Test at temperature extremes — thermal cycling causes gasket relaxation. IP ratings don't cover high-pressure water jets (use IPX5/6 for that).

IP2X>12.5mm (finger)
IP4X>1mm objects (wire)
IP5XDust protected (limited ingress)
IP6XDust tight — zero ingress
Second digit — Liquid / Water
RatingProtection
IPX1–2Dripping water (various angles)
IPX3–4Spraying / splashing water
IPX5–6Water jets (low / high pressure)
IPX7Immersion 1m / 30 min
IPX8Immersion beyond 1m (per spec)

O-Ring Seal Design for IP67
  • Groove depth: 70–75% of o-ring cross-section Ø.
  • Compression: 15–25% of cross-section.
  • For a 2mm Ø o-ring: groove depth 1.5mm, groove width 2.6mm (W = 1.3 × CS).
  • Use 70–80 Shore A NBR for water.
  • Lube with silicone grease on assembly — never petroleum-based on NBR.
  • Surface finish on sealing bore: 0.4–0.8 µm Ra (see Surface Finish sheet).
  • Verify with thermal cycle testing: −20°C to +60°C × 25 cycles before immersion test.

FAQ
  • Q: What's the difference between IP67 and IP68? IP67 = dust-tight + immersion to 1m for 30 min. IP68 = dust-tight + immersion beyond 1m at manufacturer-specified depth/duration. IP68 is technically better but the actual depth/duration is set by the manufacturer — always check the spec sheet.
  • Q: Does IP rating cover high-pressure water jets? No. IP67/68 covers immersion, not jets. For pressure washing, you need IPX5 (low pressure jet) or IPX6 (high pressure jet). IP69K covers high-pressure, high-temperature steam jets specifically.
  • Q: Can I combine ratings? (e.g., IP67 + IP69K) Yes. The full rating would be IP6K9K. The K suffix indicates modified test conditions. Many automotive and food processing products carry both IP67 and IP69K ratings.
  • Q: Does IP rating include drop protection? No. IP is only ingress protection (dust and water). Drop/impact is covered by IK ratings (IK08 = 5J, IK10 = 20J). MIL-STD-810 covers both. Consumer products often cite all three independently.
  • Q: How do I test IP67 in-house without a lab? Water bath at 1m depth for 30 min using a pressure vessel or deep bucket with a pressure gauge. For pre-qualification, use a pressurized air leak test at 0.5 bar at elevated temp (55–60°C) — catches thermal expansion issues the water bath misses.
  • Q: Do USB-C ports require a separate seal for IP67? Yes. Every port, speaker mesh, button gap, and microphone hole needs its own sealing solution. USB-C doors with gaskets are most common. Pogo pin connectors eliminate the port entirely — consider for high IP rating products.

3D Print Troubleshoot
FDM issues & common fixes
FDM first-layer adhesion: bed temp 5–10°C above Tg; first layer 80–100% flow, 50% speed. Stringing: reduce retraction distance for Bowden, increase for direct drive; dry your filament (PLA absorbs moisture in 24h open-air). Layer adhesion strength is 40–60% of XY strength — orient critical load paths in XY. PETG is more forgiving than PLA for functional parts and doesn't need enclosure.

Medical Device Materials
Biocompatibility · Sterilization · Regulatory
A material is not "medical grade" by default — the exact formulation, supplier documentation, and processing method determine qualification. The same base polymer may exist in industrial and medical-certified grades. Always verify ISO 10993 or USP Class VI status with the supplier, not just the datasheet.

Sterilization Methods
  • Steam autoclave (121–134°C): best for metals, PPSU, PEEK.
  • Restricts material choice — many plastics cannot survive repeated cycles.
  • Ethylene oxide (EtO): low-temp, suitable for heat-sensitive plastics, but requires degassing time (24–48h) and leaves toxic residue risk.
  • Gamma radiation: fast, penetrates final packaging, ideal for disposables.
  • Can embrittle or discolor some polymers over time — validate with dose mapping.
  • E-beam: similar to gamma but less penetrating — best for thin-walled devices.
  • Always qualify sterilization compatibility before design lock.
Biocompatibility Standards
  • ISO 10993 is the primary regulatory standard — covers cytotoxicity, sensitization, irritation, systemic toxicity, hemocompatibility, and implantation.
  • USP Class VI is a useful screening test but not a substitute for ISO 10993 in FDA/EU MDR submissions.
  • Testing scope must cover not just the raw material but also colorants, processing aids, surface treatments, and sterilization effects.
  • A previously tested material may still require additional testing depending on your manufacturing process.
Regulatory Pathway Considerations
  • FDA (US): Materials must be documented under 21 CFR Part 820 (QSR) including biocompatibility data, material traceability, lot numbers, and supplier qualification records.
  • EU MDR: Requires detailed material composition, biological safety data, and risk assessment documentation.
  • Always establish a full material traceability chain from raw resin supplier through processing — this is non-negotiable for audits and recalls.
  • ISO 13485 quality system expected for commercial medical device manufacturing.
Key Design Rules
  1. Use industrial-grade materials in early prototyping to save cost — switch to medical-certified grades at DVT/PVT.
  2. Specify sterilization method before material selection — this eliminates many candidates immediately.
  3. Avoid colorants unless they have documented biocompatibility — pigments are often the failure mode in ISO 10993 cytotoxicity tests.
  4. For reusable devices, design for 1,000+ sterilization cycles minimum — PPSU and PEEK are the primary choices.
  5. Surface finish matters — Ra 0.8 µm or better on any surface that contacts sterile field to prevent biofilm accumulation.
Further Reading
Fictiv — Medical Device Material Selection ↗ ISO 10993-1 Biocompatibility Standard ↗ FDA Medical Device Regulation Overview ↗ MatWeb Medical Material Database ↗
FAQ
  • Q: When do I need ISO 10993 testing? For any device that contacts the patient (directly or indirectly) for any duration. The required tests depend on contact type (surface, implant, blood) and duration (<24h, 24h–30 days, >30 days). Start with ISO 10993-1 to determine your test matrix.
  • Q: Can I use industrial-grade materials for prototypes? Yes for mechanical fit-checks and non-patient-contact prototypes. No for any clinical use, biocompatibility testing, or regulatory submission. The material grade must match the intended production material in any V&V testing.
  • Q: What's the easiest sterilization method to design for? EtO (ethylene oxide) is the most material-compatible — works with most plastics including PC and ABS. Downside: 24–48h degassing required, toxic process, harder for small volumes. Gamma is fast and scalable but degrades some polymers over time.
  • Q: How do I prove material traceability? Maintain lot-level records from raw material supplier through all processing steps. Minimum: Certificate of Analysis (CoA) with lot number, material specification, and test results. ISO 13485 quality system formalizes this requirement. Every batch used in production or clinical testing needs a traceable record.
  • Q: Is PEEK worth the cost for structural implant-adjacent parts? Yes for load-bearing ortho adjacent parts. PEEK is radiolucent (shows up clearly on MRI/CT without artifact), fully autoclavable, and has excellent biocompatibility data. At ~$200–500/kg vs $5/kg for ABS, it's expensive — but justified where performance requires it.

MIL-STD · IP · Shock · Thermal · Sealing
MIL-STD-810 is not a certification — it is a set of test methods. There is no official certifying body. "Tested to MIL-STD-810G" is self-declared. Understand which specific test methods and severities were actually run before trusting a vendor's claim.

Sealing Design for Rugged Enclosures
  • Face seal vs radial seal: face seals (gaskets) are easier to achieve at high IP ratings; radial seals (o-rings in grooves) are better for repeated assembly/disassembly.
  • For IP67: use continuous face seal, 15–25% o-ring compression, Ra 0.4–0.8 µm on mating surfaces.
  • For IP68 at depth: increase compression to 25–30% and add secondary seal or sealant bead.
  • All ports, buttons, and connectors need individual sealing solutions — USB-C with a cover and gasket is the most reliable approach.
  • Test at +60°C to catch thermal expansion seal loss before water immersion test.
Vibration and Shock Design Rules
  1. Conformal coating on PCBAs is non-negotiable for vibration environments — minimum Humiseal 1A33 at 0.05mm.
  2. Potting (PU or epoxy) for connectors and high-mass components.
  3. Avoid cantilevered PCB-mounted connectors — route vibration loads to chassis.
  4. Use thread-locking compound (Loctite 243 or equivalent) on all fasteners in vibration environments — torque + locking compound, not just torque.
  5. MIL-STD-810 shock test (Method 516) simulates 26 drops onto 2" plywood over concrete — design corners and ports as primary impact zones.
Thermal Design for Harsh Environments
  • Sealed enclosures trap heat — design for natural convection is unreliable when the vents are gasketed shut.
  • Derate all components by 20°C from datasheet max.
  • Use thermal simulations at max ambient (55–70°C) with device at full load.
  • Chassis material: die cast Al (ADC12) is the best combination of thermal conductivity and IP-friendly geometry.
  • For glass/display interfaces: polycarbonate is the lowest-risk optical bond material — surlyn and OCA optical adhesives for production.
Materials for Rugged Enclosures
MaterialDrop resist.IP?UV?Common Use
Die cast AlExcellentYesYes (anodize)Rugged handhelds, industrial tools
PC/ABS blendVery goodYesLimitedConsumer rugged, body-worn devices
ASAGoodYesExcellentOutdoor enclosures, signal housings
PolycarbonateExcellentYesPoor (yellows)Optically clear panels, windows
Overmolded TPEVery goodGasket potentialLimitedGrips, bumpers, soft-touch zones
316L SSOutstandingYesYesMarine, food-grade, medical

FAQ
  • Q: Is MIL-STD-810 a certification? No. There is no official certifying body. It is a set of test methods that manufacturers self-select and apply. "Tested to MIL-STD-810H" is a self-declaration. Always ask which specific methods (501, 514, 516, etc.) and at what severities. "MIL-STD-810 compliant" without specifics is marketing.
  • Q: What's the minimum IP rating for an outdoor consumer product? IP65 for splash/jet resistance (garden, sports). IP67 for submersion resistance (wearables, outdoor tools). IP68 for dive/swim use. For food processing or pressure washing: IP69K. Don't over-specify — each step up adds significant design and test cost.
  • Q: How do I prevent connector corrosion in outdoor products? Use sealed connectors (IP67 rated by themselves), apply conformal coat to the PCB behind the connector, use gold-plated contacts minimum for outdoor use, and design drainage paths so water doesn't pool at connectors. Amphenol, Molex, and TE make excellent IP-rated connector families.
  • Q: What conformal coat should I use? Humiseal 1A33 acrylic is the industry standard — easy to apply, reworkable, good environmental protection. For harsher environments (marine, automotive): silicone or polyurethane coat. For maximum protection: potting compound. Apply 0.05–0.13mm thickness minimum.
  • Q: How do I design for drop testing? Prioritize: corners and edges (highest stress concentration), port openings (stress risers in housing), and display-to-housing joints (glass interfaces). Use overmolded bumpers at corners. For MIL-STD-810 Method 516: 26 drops from 1.22m onto 2" plywood over concrete.

3D Printing
FDM · SLA · SLS · MJF · Process selection
3D printing is the right tool for prototyping, not for validating production intent — FDM parts have anisotropic strength (40–60% weaker in Z), different surface finish, and variable tolerances vs IM. Always note when quoting tolerances off a print.
Process Comparison
ProcessToleranceSurfaceMaterialsBest For
FDM±0.3–0.5mmRough (visible layers)PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, PA, TPUConcept models, fit checks, jigs
SLA / MSLA±0.1–0.2mmSmooth, detailedStandard, tough, flexible, castable resinsVisual prototypes, patterns for casting
SLS±0.2–0.3mmGrainy, uniformPA12, PA11, TPU, glass-fill nylonFunctional parts, hinges, complex geometry
MJF±0.2–0.3mmUniform, slightly granularPA12, PA11, TPUFunctional production volumes 1–1,000+
DMLS/SLM±0.1–0.2mmRough (needs post-processing)Ti64, 316L, AlSi10Mg, InconelComplex metal parts, aerospace, medical
Cost & Volume Guide
VolumeBest ProcessTypical $/part (simple housing)
1–10FDM or SLA$5–50
10–100SLS or MJF$15–80
100–1,000MJF or urethane cast$10–50
1,000+Injection molding$0.50–10 (+ tooling amortized)
FDM Design Rules
  • Minimum feature: 1.2mm (2× nozzle).
  • Minimum wall: 1.6mm structural, 0.8mm cosmetic.
  • Overhang: ≤45° without support.
  • Holes: add 0.2mm clearance for shafts, 0.4mm for slip fit.
  • Layer height: 0.15–0.20mm for functional parts.
  • Orient load paths in XY — Z-strength is 40–60% of XY.
  • Avoid flat surfaces parallel to bed on large parts — use chamfers to reduce warping.
  • Heat-set inserts are strongly preferred over tapped-in-plastic threads.
FDM Material Quick Reference
MaterialHDT°CNeeds enclosure?Watch out for
PLA55–60NoBrittle, creeps in heat/UV
PETG70–80NoMoisture sensitive, strings easily
ABS90–105YesWarps badly without enclosure
ASA95–100YesLike ABS but UV-stable
PA12 (Nylon)110–120YesAbsorbs moisture — dry 12h before printing
TPU 95A70NoBowden extruder struggles — use direct drive
Further Reading
Hubs FDM Design Guide ↗ Hubs SLS Design Guide ↗ Formlabs SLA Guide ↗
FAQ
  • Q: Which process gives the strongest parts? For polymer: SLS and MJF give isotropic properties (same strength in all directions). FDM is anisotropic — 40–60% weaker in Z. For metal: DMLS/SLM parts rival wrought metal after heat treatment but are highly anisotropic as-built. Always specify orientation-critical features.
  • Q: Can 3D-printed parts be used for production? Yes for SLS/MJF at volumes up to several thousand units. FDM is generally prototyping only for structural parts. DMLS for aerospace and medical production at low volume. SLA for production of small, high-detail parts (dental, jewelry patterns).
  • Q: Why are my FDM holes undersized? Plastic expands into the hole during printing. Add 0.2mm to clearance holes, 0.4mm for slip fits when designing. Alternatively, drill or ream printed holes for tight fits — this is standard practice.
  • Q: How do I get a smooth surface finish on FDM? Orient the part so cosmetic faces are on the side (not top or bottom). Increase perimeter count to 4–5 walls. Use a 0.4mm nozzle with 0.15mm layer height. For cosmetic finish: sand with 220–400 grit, prime, paint. SLA gives the best as-printed finish.
  • Q: When should I switch from 3D printing to injection molding? When: (1) volume exceeds 300–500 units, (2) material properties of printed parts are inadequate, (3) surface finish requirements can't be met post-processing, or (4) dimensional tolerance is <±0.1mm across the part. Run the numbers — tooling cost / (CNC unit cost − IM unit cost) = break-even quantity.
Further Reading
Hubs FDM Design Guide ↗ Hubs SLS Design Guide ↗ Formlabs SLA Complete Guide ↗ HP Multi Jet Fusion Technology ↗
Injection Molding
Tooling · DFM · Cost · Lead time
Break-even vs 3D printing / urethane cast is typically 300–500 units for simple parts, 1,000+ for complex multi-cavity tools. The hidden cost is design changes after T1 — each ECO on a steel tool costs $500–5,000 and 2–4 weeks. Lock geometry before releasing to tool.
Tooling Types & Cost
TypeTooling $Lead timeShotsUse case
Soft (Al) tool$3–15k1–3 wks1,000–10,000Bridge production, high EVT/DVT volume
Semi-hard (P20)$8–30k3–6 wks100,000+Medium volume, stable geometry
Production (H13)$20–100k+6–16 wks1M+High volume, textured, tight tolerance
Family tool+30–50%SameSameMultiple parts in one tool — cost effective at volume
DFM Rules
  1. Wall thickness — 1.5–4mm nominal, vary ≤25% — thicker walls = sink, warp, longer cycle time.
  2. Draft — 1° minimum untextured, 3° minimum textured (add 1° per 0.025mm texture depth).
  3. Ribs — height ≤3× wall, thickness 50–60% of wall, fillet at base.
  4. Bosses — wall 60% of nominal, gusset to base.
  5. Parting line — define explicitly on drawing — toolmaker picks worst option if unspecified.
  6. Gate location — into thick section, away from cosmetic faces and structural load areas.
  7. No undercuts unless you design in side actions or lifters — add $2–8k per action.
Tolerances
  • Commercial grade: ±0.3–0.5mm.
  • Fine grade: ±0.1–0.2mm (requires tighter process control and may need added tooling cost).
  • Critical features: specify as CTQ and request Cpk ≥1.33.
  • Tolerances are driven by material shrinkage + cooling uniformity — not just steel.
  • Verify with mold flow simulation before T1.
Common Tooling Mistakes
  1. Not specifying ejector pin locations — toolmaker puts them on cosmetic surfaces.
  2. No cosmetic zone drawing — A/B/C surface designations prevent gating, ejector, and parting line conflicts.
  3. Releasing tool before geometry is frozen — a single boss move after T1 can cost $3k and 3 weeks.
  4. Under-specifying gate type — submarine, fan, hot runner, direct — all have vestige and location implications.
  5. No texture approval before tool release — adding VDI 30 after tool cut means re-polishing and adding draft, costing significant money.
Further Reading
Hubs Injection Molding Guide ↗ Xometry IM Design Guide ↗ Protolabs IM Design Guide ↗
FAQ
  • Q: How do I eliminate sink marks? The root cause is almost always wall thickness variation. Core out thick sections to match nominal wall. Keep ribs at 50–60% of wall thickness. If you can't change geometry, move the gate closer to the thick section so it packs out first.
  • Q: What's causing my part to warp? Uneven cooling (asymmetric wall thickness, poor cooling channel layout), semicrystalline material shrinkage (PP, Nylon, POM warp more than ABS/PC), or insufficient cooling time. Fix in order: wall uniformity → gate location → cooling channel design → process parameters.
  • Q: How do I prevent weld lines on cosmetic surfaces? Weld lines form where two flow fronts meet. Reposition the gate so flow fronts meet in a non-cosmetic area. Use flow simulation to predict weld line location before cutting steel. You can also increase melt and mold temp to improve weld line strength.
  • Q: When do I need a hot runner vs cold runner? Cold runner for simple parts, low cavitation, or when you want to save tool cost. Hot runner eliminates runner waste (important for expensive resins), gives better gate control, and is standard for multi-cavity high-volume production. Hot runner adds $5–20k to tooling cost.
  • Q: Can I add ribs to increase stiffness without sinking? Yes, but keep rib thickness at 50–60% of nominal wall (not more). Height max 3× wall. Use multiple thin ribs rather than one thick rib. Fillet at the base (r ≥ 0.25mm minimum). Sink marks will appear on the cosmetic opposite face if you violate these rules.
  • Q: What's the minimum draft angle for texture? 1° per 0.025mm of texture depth as a rule of thumb. VDI 18 texture (medium grain): 3° min. VDI 30 (coarse grain): 5° min. Not enough draft on texture = drag marks, sticking parts, and rapid tool wear. Specify texture and draft together.
Further Reading
Hubs Injection Molding Design Guide ↗ Xometry IM Design Guide ↗ Super-Ingenuity — IM Engineering Guide ↗ Zetar — Injection Molding Defects Guide ↗
CNC Machining
Milling · Turning · EDM · Tolerances
At prototype volumes, 60–70% of your CNC cost is setup and programming — not cutting time. Design parts that fixture in a standard vise with minimal setups. 3-axis is 3–5× cheaper than 5-axis — 5-axis is only justified when geometry demands it.
Process Types
ProcessToleranceBest ForLimitations
3-axis milling±0.025–0.1mmPrismatic parts, pockets, slotsUndercuts require repositioning
5-axis milling±0.013–0.05mmComplex contours, impellers, aero parts3–5× more expensive
CNC turning±0.01–0.05mmShafts, bushings, round partsRotational geometry only
Wire EDM±0.003–0.01mmTight-tolerance 2D profiles, hard metalsSlow, conductive materials only
Sinker EDM±0.005–0.025mmDeep cavities, tooling, blind featuresSlow, requires electrode design
DFM Rules
  1. Avoid sharp internal corners — specify minimum corner radius = tool radius + 20% clearance. Rule of thumb: r ≥ 0.5× pocket depth.
  2. Minimum feature size — 0.5mm for milled features, 0.3mm for turned features.
  3. Deep slots — width ≥ 1.5× depth — deeper than this requires special tooling and significantly increases cost.
  4. Thin walls — minimum 0.8mm for Al, 1.0mm for steel — thinner walls vibrate during cutting and produce poor finish.
  5. Avoid specifying tighter tolerance than needed — ±0.025mm costs 3–5× more than ±0.1mm. Only CTQ features need tight tolerances.
  6. Thread depths — 1.5× diameter min in steel, 2× in aluminum.
Material Machinability
MaterialMachinabilityTool wearCost index
6061-T6 AlExcellentLow1.0×
7075-T6 AlVery goodLow-medium1.3×
303 SSGoodMedium2.5×
316L SSFair (gummy)High3.5×
4140 HTGoodMedium-high2.0×
Ti-6Al-4VPoorVery high5–8×
PEEKGoodLow2.0× (material cost dominates)
Further Reading
Hubs CNC Design Guide ↗ Xometry CNC Design Guide ↗
FAQ
  • Q: What tolerance should I spec if I don't know? Use ±0.1mm (approximately ISO IT9) as your drawing default for non-critical features. Only tighten where there's a functional reason. Most CNC shops default to ±0.1mm if you don't specify — confirm this with your shop before assuming.
  • Q: Why does tighter tolerance cost so much more? Slower feeds/speeds, more finishing passes, different tooling, and more time-consuming inspection. ±0.025mm is roughly 3–5× more expensive than ±0.1mm. ±0.01mm may require temperature-controlled environment and CMM inspection. Only specify what the function requires.
  • Q: Can CNC hold ±0.005mm? Yes, on small features in aluminum, on a precision mill with temperature control. Not consistently on large features, in steel, or without careful setup. For ±0.005mm and below: discuss with your shop before designing to it. You may need grinding instead of milling.
  • Q: Does aluminum expand enough to matter? Yes at high precision. 6061-T6 thermal expansion: 23.6 µm/m·°C. A 200mm part changes 0.047mm per 10°C. Inspect precision parts at 20°C per ISO 1 standard. Dowel holes across mating plates should use the same material to minimize differential expansion.
  • Q: What file format should I send? STEP (.stp) for the 3D model. PDF drawing with GD&T callouts, surface finish, material, and tolerances. Always send a drawing — never rely on the model alone for manufacturing intent. The drawing is the legal document.
  • Q: What's the best way to reduce CNC cost? Reduce setups (design for 2-op max). Avoid deep narrow slots. Don't specify tight tolerances where unnecessary. Use standard drill/tap sizes (avoid custom tooling). Increase batch size. Design for standard stock sizes to minimize raw material waste.
Further Reading
Hubs CNC Design Guide ↗ RivCut — CNC Tolerance Reference ↗ FiveFlute — CNC Tolerance First Principles ↗
Sheet Metal
Bending · Laser · Punching · Forming
Sheet metal tooling is cheap ($500–5k for simple brackets) vs injection molding ($10k+). At 50–5,000 units, sheet metal is almost always the right choice for enclosures, brackets, and chassis. Design parts to nest on a standard sheet to minimize material waste.
Process Overview
ProcessToleranceSetup costBest For
Laser cutting±0.1–0.2mmLow ($0–200)Flat profiles, cutouts, prototyping
Punching / turret±0.1–0.25mmMedium ($200–2k)High-volume flat profiles with standard features
Press brake bending±0.5–1° angleLow (tooling amortized)Flanges, brackets, enclosure panels
Progressive die stamp±0.05–0.2mm$5–50kVery high volume, complex formed shapes
Deep drawing±0.1–0.3mm$3–20kCans, cups, shells — axisymmetric forms
Bend Design Rules
  • Minimum bend radius: 1× material thickness for steel, 1.5× for aluminum, 0.5× for Cu/brass.
  • K-factor: 0.44 for steel, 0.41 for aluminum (used in flat pattern calculation).
  • Minimum flange length: 4× material thickness (to allow tooling clearance).
  • Hole-to-bend distance: ≥2× material thickness + bend radius — closer holes distort on bending.
  • Relief cuts at intersecting bends to prevent tearing.
  • Minimum feature size in laser cutting: 1× material thickness.
Common Materials
MaterialThickness rangeNotes
1008/1010 CRS0.5–6mmMost common — good formability, weldable
304 Stainless0.5–6mmCorrosion resistant, work-hardens quickly — use larger bend radius
316L Stainless0.5–4mmMarine/medical — pricier, more difficult to form
5052 Al0.5–6mmBest formability of Al alloys for sheet work
6061 Al0.8–6mmStronger but cracks on tight bends — anneal or use larger radius
Further Reading
Hubs Sheet Metal Guide ↗ Xometry Sheet Metal DFM ↗
FAQ
  • Q: How accurate is bend angle in practice? Press brake bending: ±0.5–1° typical. For tighter angles, specify a secondary coining operation (±0.25°) or design in an adjustment mechanism. Springback varies by material and thickness — your CM should compensate, but verify in first article.
  • Q: What's minimum hole diameter near a bend? Keep holes at least 2× material thickness + bend radius away from the bend centerline. Closer than this and the hole will distort during bending. If you need a hole close to a bend, punch it after bending.
  • Q: Can I anodize sheet metal? Only aluminum. 5052 and 6061 anodize well. Note: cut edges won't anodize as well as rolled surfaces. For cosmetic anodized sheet metal, design so cut edges are hidden or masked.
  • Q: What's the flatness tolerance of laser-cut sheet metal? Raw sheet: ±0.5–1mm flatness on a 300mm panel depending on thickness and alloy. Laser cutting introduces heat that can bow thin sheets. For flatness-critical applications, specify a leveling operation or design in stiffening ribs.
  • Q: When is progressive die stamping worth it? At >10,000 units per year for a part that can be formed from a single strip. Die cost: $15–100k. Per-part cost at volume: $0.05–2. Lead time: 8–20 weeks. Breakeven vs press brake: typically 5,000–20,000 units depending on part complexity.
Further Reading
Hubs Sheet Metal Design Guide ↗ Xometry Sheet Metal DFM Guide ↗ Trumpf Laser Cutting Resources ↗
Urethane / Vacuum Casting
RTV silicone · Bridge production · Low volume
Urethane casting is the best bridge between 3D printing and injection molding: production-representative surface finish and material properties, 2–3 week lead time, no hard tooling. A single SLA master + RTV mold gets you 20–50 parts. Best for 20–500 unit runs.
Process Overview
  • A high-quality master pattern (usually SLA or CNC) is used to create a silicone RTV mold under vacuum.
  • Two-part polyurethane resin is poured into the mold under vacuum to eliminate bubbles.
  • Each mold yields 20–50 castings depending on complexity before silicone degrades.
  • Silicone molds cost $400–1,500 each.
  • Per-part cost: $15–150 depending on size and complexity.
  • Lead time: 2–3 weeks for first parts, repeat orders in days.
Urethane Material Options
Urethane typeShoreSimulatesNotes
Rigid (Smooth-On 65D)65DABS / PCGood for housings, structural parts
Semi-rigid80A–60DPP / soft ABSSnap fits, flexible enclosures
Flexible40A–80ATPE / soft rubberGaskets, grips, overmold simulation
Clear70DPC / PMMALenses, display windows (optical clarity limited)
High-temp65DHigh-temp ABSUp to 130°C — functional thermal testing
Design Considerations
  • Tolerance: ±0.3–0.5mm typical — not as tight as CNC or IM.
  • Draft: 1–3° recommended for mold release.
  • Texture: silicone picks up surface detail from master — SLA master gives best cosmetic result.
  • Thin walls: minimum 0.8mm.
  • Avoid deep blind holes — air trapping causes voids.
  • Insert metals (M3+ heat-set or threaded inserts) before casting by embedding in the mold.
  • Color: achieved with pigment — color consistency is harder to control than IM.
When to Use
  1. Pre-launch marketing samples and customer review units.
  2. Functional DVT parts while waiting for production tooling.
  3. Low-volume products where injection mold tooling cost is not justified (< 500 lifetime units).
  4. Multi-color and over-molded appearance models.
  5. Not recommended for — tight-tolerance mechanical assemblies, high-temp applications >130°C, or parts requiring FDA/ISO certified material traceability.
Further Reading
Fictiv Urethane Casting Guide ↗ Smooth-On Material Tutorials ↗
FAQ
  • Q: How many parts can I get from one silicone mold? 20–50 shots per mold is typical. Molds degrade from heat, resin chemistry, and mechanical stress. Complex parts with undercuts degrade faster. For 50+ parts, plan for a second mold or a more durable tooling material.
  • Q: Can urethane casting match injection-molded surface finish? Yes for cosmetic surfaces — silicone picks up every detail from the master. Use an SLA master for the best result. The difference is internal: IM parts have better mechanical properties, tighter tolerances, and no parting line artifacts on complex undercuts.
  • Q: What urethane for a functional prototype? Smooth-On VytaFlex 60 or PMC-790 for rigid structural parts (simulates ABS). Smooth-On PMC-121/30 for flexible parts (simulates TPU). Shore D 65 rigid urethanes are the most common for housing prototypes. Always test actual mechanical properties before assuming equivalence.
  • Q: Is vacuum casting the same as urethane casting? Vacuum casting is urethane casting done under vacuum — the mold and resin are both degassed in a vacuum chamber before pouring. This eliminates bubbles and gives better surface quality. All professional urethane casting services use vacuum; "urethane casting" and "vacuum casting" are often used interchangeably.

Overmolding
2-shot · Insert · Substrate compatibility
Chemical adhesion between overmold and substrate is always preferred over mechanical interlocking alone. Test adhesion on a flat coupon before committing to tooling. Poor adhesion is the #1 cause of overmold delamination in field returns.
Process Types
TypeHowToolingBest For
2-shot (2K) moldingBoth materials in one machine, one cycleRotating platen tool — 2× tooling costHigh volume, tight registration, best adhesion
Insert overmoldingSubstrate placed in B-tool, overmold injectedSeparate toolsLower volume, substrate from different supplier
Dip/spray coatingSubstrate dipped or sprayed with elastomerNoneVery thin coatings, grips, handles
Substrate / Overmold Compatibility
SubstrateCompatible overmoldBond typeAdhesion
ABSTPE, TPU, soft PVCChemical + mechanicalExcellent
PCTPE, TPUChemical + mechanicalVery good
PC/ABS blendTPE, TPUChemical + mechanicalExcellent
Nylon (PA6/66)TPE-PA basedChemicalGood (match PA-based TPE)
PPTPE-PP based (SEBS)ChemicalGood — requires PP-compatible TPE specifically
Metal insertsAny overmoldMechanical (undercuts)Good with proper geometry
DFM Rules
  1. Substrate wall under overmold — 1.5mm minimum to resist injection pressure.
  2. Overmold wall — 1.2–3mm — too thin doesn't fill, too thick causes sink on substrate.
  3. Add mechanical interlocks (holes, undercuts, ribs) even when chemical bond is expected — belt and suspenders.
  4. Corner radii on substrate — 0.5mm minimum where overmold wraps — sharp corners cause adhesion failure and stress concentration.
  5. Gate overmold into thick section, not at a thin edge.
  6. Avoid texturing substrate at overmold interface — smooth substrate promotes chemical bond; texture creates air pockets.
Further Reading
Fictiv — Overmolding Compatibility Guide ↗ Kraiburg TPE Adhesion Guide ↗
FAQ
  • Q: Why does my overmold peel off? Almost always one of: wrong TPE chemistry for the substrate (PP substrate needs PP-based SEBS, not generic TPE), substrate surface contamination (oils, mold release), substrate too cold during overmolding, or insufficient wall thickness preventing adequate bond area.
  • Q: Can I overmold onto metal? Yes, but only mechanically — there's no chemical adhesion between urethane/TPE and metal. Design undercuts, holes, and knurled surfaces on the metal insert for mechanical interlocking. The overmold grips the geometry, not the material.
  • Q: What's the minimum overmold wall thickness? 1.2mm is the practical minimum for most TPE/TPU overmolds. Below this: inconsistent fill, potential breakthrough to the substrate, and poor cosmetic result. Target 1.5–3mm for reliable bonding and appearance.
  • Q: 2-shot or insert overmolding? 2-shot (2K) for high volume (>10,000 units) — better bond, tighter registration, one cycle. Insert overmolding for lower volume or when the substrate comes from a different supplier/process. 2K tooling costs roughly 2× a standard single-material tool.
Further Reading
Fictiv — Overmolding Compatibility Guide ↗ Kraiburg TPE — Substrate Adhesion Guide ↗ Hubs Overmolding Guide ↗
Die Casting
Al · Zn · Mg · Tooling · Cost
Die casting gives tighter dimensional control than injection molding for metal parts at volume. Tooling is expensive ($20–150k) but per-part cost is very low at 5,000+ units. The critical DFM rule: uniform wall thickness — thin/thick junctions cause porosity, which kills structural integrity and pressure-tight requirements.
Alloy Comparison
AlloyUTS MPaρ g/ccTooling lifeBest For
ADC12 (Al)3102.74100–300k shotsEnclosures, structural — most common die cast Al
A380 (Al)3242.76100–300k shotsUS equivalent of ADC12, automotive and consumer
ZA-8 (Zn-Al)3746.3500k–1M shotsSmall precision parts, connectors, decorative
Zamak 3 (Zn)2836.6500k–1M shotsMost common Zn alloy — excellent surface finish
AZ91D (Mg)2501.81150–300k shotsLightest structural option — laptop chassis, auto
DFM Rules
  • Wall thickness: 2–4mm for Al, 1–2.5mm for Zn, 1.5–4mm for Mg.
  • Uniform walls are critical — porosity forms at thick/thin junctions during solidification.
  • Draft angles: 1–3° minimum on all vertical surfaces.
  • Undercuts require slides adding $3–10k per action.
  • Radius all corners: minimum R0.5mm external, R1.0mm internal — sharp corners are stress risers and cause die erosion.
  • Tolerances: ±0.1–0.3mm typical.
  • Secondary machining operations (CNC bores, tapped holes) are very common — design bosses for secondary ops.
Cost Model
ItemRangeNotes
Tooling (single cavity)$20–80kComplexity and alloy dependent
Part cost at 5k units$2–15Al alloy, medium complexity
Part cost at 50k units$0.50–5Tooling fully amortized
Secondary machining+$0.50–5/partBore holes, tapped features, critical faces
FAQ
  • Q: Why does die casting have porosity? Trapped air and gas from turbulent metal injection. Design uniform walls, avoid thick/thin junctions. Specify vacuum-assist for structural parts. Porosity makes parts non-weldable and reduces fatigue strength.
  • Q: Can I tap threads directly in a die casting? Yes for non-critical threads. For critical: design a machining boss and drill/tap in secondary CNC op. Die cast holes need secondary drilling before tapping for best results.
  • Q: What alloy for an outdoor enclosure? ADC12 with Type III hard anodize for most outdoor use. For coastal/marine add sealant. Zinc gives excellent surface finish but lower corrosion resistance — best for indoor precision parts.
  • Q: How thin can walls go? Min 1.5mm Al, 0.8mm Zn. Below this: inconsistent fill and porosity. Zinc allows thinner walls due to better fluidity at lower temps.
  • Q: When does die casting beat machining? Complex metal geometry at >5,000 units. Also when EMI shielding, thermal conductivity, or structural stiffness is needed in a complex enclosure shape that would be expensive to machine.
