Fictiv Die Casting Guide ↗ NADCA Die Casting FAQ ↗
Other Processes
Thermoforming · Extrusion · Blow · Compression
These processes are less commonly used in consumer hardware but are dominant in packaging, medical tubing, industrial enclosures, and high-volume automotive. Understanding when to specify each saves significant cost and lead time at scale.
Thermoforming
  • A plastic sheet is heated and formed over or into a mold under vacuum or pressure.
  • Tooling cost: $500–15k (Al or composite molds — far cheaper than IM).
  • Tolerances: ±0.5–2mm.
  • Wall thickness: uniform input sheet, varies in formed part — thins at deep draws and sharp corners.
  • Best for: packaging inserts, large enclosure panels, medical trays, display bezels.
  • Design rules: draft 3–5°, avoid deep draws (>1× diameter), limit sharp corners.
  • Materials: ABS, PETG, PC, HDPE, PVC.
  • Production rate: 200–2,000 parts/hr at volume.
Extrusion
  • Molten plastic or metal is pushed through a shaped die to produce continuous profiles.
  • Tooling cost: $1–10k per die.
  • Best for: tubes, channels, frames, seals, wire insulation, window profiles.
  • Cross-section is constant — design complexity is in the die, not the part length.
  • Materials: Al 6063 (architectural profiles), PVC, PE, PP, TPE (medical tubing), silicone (seals).
  • Tolerances: ±0.1–0.5mm on profile dimensions, ±1mm on length (secondary cutting).
  • Secondary operations: cut, drill, punch, bend for finished parts.
Blow Molding
  • A plastic parison (tube) is inflated with air inside a mold to form hollow shapes.
  • Best for: bottles, containers, hollow automotive parts, medical fluid containers.
  • Three types: extrusion blow (EBM) for HDPE/PP bottles, injection blow (IBM) for high-precision pharmaceutical containers, stretch blow (ISBM) for PET bottles.
  • Tooling: $5–50k.
  • Wall thickness control: good on cylindrical forms, poor on complex contours.
  • Minimum wall: 0.5mm for PET, 1.0mm for HDPE.
  • Not suitable for: parts with internal features, tight dimensional tolerances, or structural load paths.
Compression Molding
  • Material charge (thermoset, rubber, or SMC) is placed in an open mold, then pressed closed under heat and pressure.
  • Best for: rubber seals and gaskets, electrical insulators, automotive panels (SMC/BMC), large composite structures.
  • Advantages over injection molding: lower pressure = cheaper tooling for large parts, works with thermosets and rubber that can't be injection molded, minimal wasted material.
  • Disadvantages: longer cycle time, more labor-intensive, flash trimming required.
  • Tolerances: ±0.3–1mm.
  • Materials: NBR/EPDM/silicone rubber, phenolic, epoxy SMC, UHMWPE.
Process Selection Summary
If you need...Consider
Hollow container, bottleBlow molding (ISBM for PET, EBM for HDPE)
Large flat panel (>400mm), low costThermoforming
Continuous profile (tube, channel)Extrusion
Rubber gasket, seal, large matCompression molding
Complex 3D plastic shape, high volumeInjection molding

Tuesday Teardown
Weekly DFM · Annotated
This Week · Issue #001
Logitech MX Master 3 Scroll Wheel
Electromagnetic MagSpeed mechanism · 5 parts · Zero friction bearings
DFM Annotation #1 — Rotor Hub
Insert-molded brass hub into PP rotor body. Why: Eliminates separate assembly step. Boss OD is exactly 2× insert OD — textbook rule. Draft on spokes is 1.5° despite thin walls, showing the mold opens axially not radially. Clever parting line placement avoids any side-action cost.
DFM Annotation #2 — Electromagnetic Brake
Copper coil is wound on a bobbin, not bare — allows automated winding and eliminates manual insulation. The bobbin snaps onto the frame with a single clip: zero fasteners, zero tools. Designed for sub-30-second robotic assembly. This is what Design for Assembly (DFA) looks like in production.
DFM Annotation #3 — Housing Snap
The main housing uses a 4-point cantilever snap strategy — no screws visible externally. Each snap has a 30° lead-in angle and 90° retention angle (not 45°) making it a near-permanent snap by intent. Wall thickness behind snaps is 1.8mm vs 2.4mm nominal — slightly thinner to increase flex without compromising OA rigidity. Controlled by rib support 3mm back from the snap face.
Injection Molding
Insert Molding

Previous · Issue #000
Apple AirTag — 4 parts, 1 screw
CR2032 holder · Waterproofing · Twist-lock shell
Key DFM Insight
The twist-lock lid eliminates all external fasteners. IP67 is achieved with a single molded silicone gasket that compresses axially — no groove machining, no secondary assembly. The entire product assembles in one rotational motion. At >30M units, even 0.5 seconds of assembly time saved = $4M+ annually at $0.25/labor-minute. This is what scale-optimized DFM looks like.

Thread engagement rule: 1.5× diameter for steel, 2× for aluminum
After years of watching warranty returns and stripped threads: 1.5D engagement in steel is safe. In aluminum you need 2D minimum, and in plastic go 3D or use a heat-set insert. This one rule eliminates 80% of the thread stripping failures I see.

CNC setup cost is often larger than machining time — design for common fixturing
At prototype volumes, 60–70% of your CNC cost is setup and programming, not cutting. Designing parts that can be fixtured in a standard vise — flat datum face, no undercuts, accessible features — can cut quote prices by 30–40%. 5-axis is only worth it if geometry demands it.

Spec Tip
HW Eng · Dallas
1d
Always specify color by Pantone, RAL, and CIELAB — not just a name
Specifying "matte black" gets you 40 different results across 5 suppliers. A proper color spec: Pantone 419 C, RAL 9005, L*=20 ±1 a*=0 ±0.5 b*=0 ±0.5 measured with D65 illuminant at 10° observer. Costs nothing to write. Prevents endless rounds of color approval.

FC
Frank C.
Spec Tip
Product Eng · LA
3d
Specify torque AND angle for critical fasteners, not just torque alone
Torque-only specs have ±30% scatter due to lubrication and surface finish variation. Torque + angle (e.g. 8 N·m + 90°) reduces scatter to ±5%. For battery connectors, seat sensors, and anything safety-adjacent — use angle. Add it to your manufacturing process spec sheet.

Hardness after machining vs before — specify both on the drawing
Found this out after a batch of 4140 shafts came back from the CM at HRC 28 when we needed HRC 40–45. The drawing said "4140 HRC 40–45" but didn't specify when to measure. CM machined soft stock, skipped heat treat. Two callouts: stock condition and post-processing hardness.

Spec Tip
ME · Portland
1w
Silicone vs NBR o-rings: the decision is temperature, not cost
NBR: −30°C to +100°C, good chemical resistance, cheap. Silicone: −60°C to +200°C, poor abrasion resistance, 3× cost. If your operating range is entirely within NBR limits, use NBR. The silicone upsell from suppliers is usually unnecessary. EPDM is the right call for outdoor/UV exposure, not silicone.

IP67 field failures, root cause was not water pressure
our IP67 product started failing in the field at month 3-4. passed every DVT test. spent weeks chasing it. turned out the housing was expanding enough in summer heat that o-ring compression dropped below the minimum. designed for static, not thermal cycling. v2 has extra compression margin and a secondary bead. posting this so someone else doesnt have to go through it
